unitDescription.value: In this unit, students investigate how data can be used to monitor performance, evaluate progress, and make informed decisions in a sports science context. Using micro:bits as data collection devices, students gather quantitative data from physical activities and import it into Microsoft Excel for organisation, analysis, and visualisation. Students apply formulas, charts, and data modelling techniques to identify trends, compare performance over time, and evaluate the effectiveness of training or testing strategies. Through increasingly independent investigations, students use evidence from their data to justify conclusions and make recommendations for improving performance, reinforcing the role of digital technologies in solving real-world problems.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: The Years 9–10 cohort consists of a diverse group of boys with a wide range of digital competencies, from students with strong technical skills and personal interest in IT, to those who require further support to confidently engage with digital systems. Many students come from regional or rural backgrounds, where access to structured digital learning opportunities may have been limited. The program is designed to build on prior knowledge while introducing more advanced and applied skills relevant to future study and employment. The curriculum supports the school’s priority to equip students with transferable digital skills, critical thinking abilities, and an understanding of ethical technology use in a rapidly changing world.

description.value: In this unit, students apply computational thinking and systems design to the field of sports science, using the Micro:bit V2 as an integrated data acquisition tool. Students decompose athletic performance requirements into specific metrics, designing and implementing object-oriented solutions to capture, process, and log physiological and movement data. The unit emphasises data integrity, requiring students to clean, validate, and query structured datasets to derive actionable insights. Through the development of interactive visualisations and dashboards, students model performance trends and evaluate their systems against established user stories and design criteria. Ethical considerations regarding data privacy and the future impact of wearable technologies are critiqued, aligning with the school’s focus on transferable digital skills and analytical rigour.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students develop and modify innovative digital solutions, decompose real-world problems, and critically evaluate alternative solutions against stakeholder elicited user stories. Students acquire, interpret and model complex data with databases and represent documents as content, structure and presentation. They design and validate algorithms and implement them, including in an object-oriented programming language. Students explain how digital systems manage, control and secure access to data; and model cyber security threats and explore a vulnerability. They use advanced features of digital tools to create interactive content, and to plan, collaborate on, and manage agile projects. Students apply privacy principles to manage digital footprints.

question: How might the micro:bit's memory ceiling specifically impact high-frequency sampling during a sprint?
expected: High-frequency sampling generates large data packets that exceed the 32KB RAM quickly, potentially causing data loss or system crashes if not streamed in real-time.
question: Why is the accelerometer range (e.g., ±2g vs ±16g) a critical factor when selecting hardware for high-impact sports?
expected: If the impact force exceeds the sensor's sensitivity range (g-force), the data will clip or max out, resulting in inaccurate or incomplete readings of the athlete's peak acceleration.

activities.title: Decomposition Vocabulary and Key Concepts
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the methodology of computational thinking applied to sports science. Model the breakdown of a vague requirement, such as 'monitor rugby tackle efficiency', by demonstrating how it must be decomposed into measurable variables like 'impact force (Newtons)', 'shoulder angle (degrees)', and 'time to contact (milliseconds)'. Explain that stakeholders, such as the Yeppoon Seagulls coaching staff, have distinct needs compared to players.
activities.studentsDo: Engage with the provided cloze passage to formalise their understanding of problem decomposition. Use the word bank to correctly identify the terminology required to define sports technology systems.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the cloze exercise by selecting the correct term from the word bank to fill in each numbered gap in the sentences below.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must we decompose a broad sports coaching request into smaller parts?
expected: To identify exact sensor requirements and isolate specific, measurable metrics that hardware like a micro:bit can capture accurately.
question: How do athlete and coach stakeholder needs differ in a sports monitoring system?
expected: Athletes prioritize non-functional requirements like comfort, durability, and wearable ergonomics; coaches prioritize functional requirements like metric accuracy, data visualization, and accessibility.
activities.scaffolding: Problem Decomposition: Breaking a complex system into smaller, manageable sub-problems. Stakeholder: An individual with a vested interest or role in the system (e.g., coaches, athletes, trainers). Functional Requirement: A specific behaviour or data output the system must produce to satisfy the user goal. Non-functional Requirement: Constraints on the system, such as portability, weight, or battery life.

activities.transition: Upon completion, students transition to the 'Stakeholder Interview' worksheet to apply these terms to a practical scenario.

question: What might happen if we ignore athlete comfort requirements when designing a micro:bit housing?
expected: Athletes may refuse to wear the device, or the housing may alter their natural biomechanics (e.g., changing their tackle technique to protect the device), leading to corrupt or unrepresentative data integrity.
question: Why does a sports scientist require different data than a head coach?
expected: Coaches require actionable, summarized performance insights for decision-making (e.g., fatigue levels), whereas scientists require granular, raw data for longitudinal analysis and validation of the measurement methods.

activities.studentsDo: Select an athletic movement (e.g., rugby pass speed, sprint acceleration, or tackle impact). activities.questioning:
question: How does measuring 'time in the air' mathematically validate a vertical leap height?
expected: Using the kinematic formula h = 1/8 g t^2, where t is the duration between takeoff and landing states, allows for direct height calculation based on gravity constants.
question: Why must a decomposition identify non-functional requirements like 'sensor sensitivity' alongside functional metrics?
expected: Because sensors have noise floors; if the sensitivity is too low, the device may fail to register the 'Takeoff' phase, leading to incomplete data capture regardless of the code accuracy.

activities.title: User Story Anatomy and Modeling
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the agile user story syntax: 'As a [stakeholder], I want to [feature/action] so that [benefit/outcome]'. Use the example of a rugby training sensor: 'As a St Brendan's College Rugby coach, I want to track player heart rate data during high-intensity interval training, so that I can monitor athlete exertion levels and prevent over-training.' Demonstrate how to unpack these three components.
activities.studentsDo: Identify and annotate the 'role', 'action', and 'benefit' components within the provided exemplar in the workbook. Students follow the modelling to deconstruct the rugby coaching scenario into the required agile structure.
activities.visibleInstructions: Annotate the provided user story in your workbook by circling the three core components: Role, Action, and Benefit. Ensure your definitions align with the St Brendan's College sports technology context.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is the 'so that' clause critical in a user story?
expected: It identifies the specific business or athletic value, ensuring the technology solution serves a measurable performance outcome rather than just collecting raw data.
question: What happens if a user story omits the 'role' component?
expected: The developer lacks context regarding the user's specific requirements or skill level, leading to a tool that may be too complex or too basic for the target audience.
activities.scaffolding:
Anatomy Guide: 
1. Role: Who is the user? (e.g., Coach, Athlete, Sports Scientist)
2. Action: What feature is needed? (e.g., Calculate, Log, Monitor, Export)
3. Benefit: Why is this valuable? (e.g., Reduce injury risk, Optimize training load, Analyze technical form)
Template: As a [User], I want to [Action], so that [Benefit].
activities.eLearning: Direct students to access the workbook via the classroom portal; maintain focus on physical annotation during the modelling phase.
activities.transition: Transition students from this modelling phase into the 'we-do' section where they co-construct user stories based on Livingstone Shire Council local sports facility criteria.

activities.teacherDoes: Model the 'As a... I want to... so that...' structure by leading a collaborative drafting session on the whiteboard. Using the example of a school rugby player, demonstrate how to turn a vague requirement ('we need to track speed') into a precise user story: 'As a St Brendan's rugby player, I want to record my peak acceleration in meters per second squared, so that I can compare my output against team benchmarks.' Emphasize that the 'so that' clause must relate directly to a measurable performance improvement.
activities.studentsDo: Engage in the guided co-construction exercise. Using the provided workbook template, follow along to draft two user stories: one for a sprinter measuring stride frequency and one for a swimmer measuring lap turnaround times. Work with a partner to verify that each story contains all three components of the user story framework.

activities.questioning: Why must the 'I want to' clause define a specific technical capability? Expected: It clarifies the functional requirement for the hardware or software, such as 'tracking cadence' versus 'tracking speed.' How does the 'so that' clause assist in the evaluation of our project? Expected: It defines the 'why' or the success criteria, allowing us to test if the measurement actually improves performance.

activities.title: Design Criteria Vocabulary and Definitions
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly distinguish between functional requirements (what the system does: data logging accuracy, CSV export) and non-functional requirements (how the system behaves: weight, durability, battery life). Model the matching logic by thinking aloud: 'If a requirement defines a specific calculation, it is functional. If it defines a physical limitation, it is non-functional.' activities.questioning: 1. Why is battery longevity considered a non-functional requirement? If a device fails to export data in CSV format, has a functional or non-functional requirement been breached? Expected: Functional, as the capability to perform specific data processing is missing.
activities.scaffolding: Functional Requirement: A measurable or specific operational capability the device must perform (e.g., 'The device shall log jump height in millimetres'). Non-Functional Requirement: A quality, constraint, or 'attribute' of the system (e.g., 'The device must be water-resistant to IP67 standards').

Model how to check a device against the checklist: 'We tick 'Battery pack security' only if the mounting solution prevents disconnection during high-impact rugby contact; otherwise, this becomes a project failure point.'
activities.studentsDo: Evaluate the proposed wearable device specification against the provided micro:bit V2 hardware constraints checklist. Tick features that meet the technical requirements for field deployment and provide a brief justification for why each is critical for sports data integrity.

question: What limitation does the micro:bit V2 have regarding continuous data logging without a PC connection?
expected: Limited onboard RAM and flash memory mean the device cannot store large datasets locally for extended periods, necessitating real-time radio transmission to a base station.
question: Why is the sampling rate a critical constraint for athletic performance analysis?
expected: Lower sampling rates (below 50Hz) may miss rapid athletic movements like sudden changes of direction or impact forces, leading to inaccurate performance metrics.

1. Onboard Memory: Limited storage capacity for data logs. 
2. Sampling Rate: The frequency of sensor data acquisition (measured in Hertz).

activities.title: Core Terminology and Logical Operators
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the function of logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) using the Micro:bit accelerometer threshold of 2048 mg. Model the logic: 'If acceleration > 2048 AND impact == true, THEN increment counter'. Provide a concrete example on the whiteboard demonstrating how the NOT operator prevents 'double-counting' by inverting the state of a cooldown timer.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the 'Logical Operations Table' by matching the operator to its functional definition and then documenting the threshold logic for a standard impact sensor in the definition table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the table by matching the logical operator to its correct definition. Use the provided bank to assist your selection.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the primary difference between the AND operator and the OR operator when tracking athlete movement?
expected: AND requires multiple conditions (e.g., speed and impact) to be simultaneously satisfied, whereas OR allows for any single condition to trigger the event.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. Global variables are essential for tracking cumulative sports performance metrics because they maintain their state and value throughout the program's execution, persisting across multiple function calls. This ensures that data, such as a running total of impacts or the highest recorded peak acceleration, is not reset or lost when a function completes. For instance, to record the maximum G-force detected during a session, the `max_g_force` variable must be global, allowing any function detecting a new peak to update this persistent record.

2. For raw accelerometer values directly from the Micro:bit (e.g., `accelerometer.get_x()`), integer data types are generally sufficient and preferable. The Micro:bit's accelerometer typically reports values as whole numbers (milligravities), making integers efficient for storage and processing on resource-constrained devices. This conserves memory and processing cycles, which is critical for high-frequency sensor readings. However, if the application requires precise calibration factors, conversion to standard units (e.g., meters per second squared), or complex calculations involving decimal points, then floating-point data types would be necessary to maintain numerical accuracy. The choice depends on the required precision and the computational demands.

activities.teacherAnswerKey:
1. 'on start' block (Initialisation): This block executes once at program startup, typically used to declare and initialise variables, calibrate sensors, or set up display elements, establishing a known baseline state for the program. This is crucial for consistent data collection.
2. 'forever' block (Main Program Loop): This block executes continuously after the 'on start' block completes, facilitating real-time data acquisition, processing, and output. It is fundamental for ongoing sports metric monitoring that requires constant sensor readings and logic evaluation.
3. Conditional Statement ('if...then'): This block evaluates a boolean expression (e.g., sensor value > threshold), directing program flow based on whether the condition is met. It directly maps to decision diamonds in a flowchart, enabling specific actions based on detected sport event parameters.
4. Data Output ('serial write line'): This statement transmits processed data or status messages via the serial port, allowing for real-time monitoring and logging of sport metric outcomes on a connected computer. It is vital for verifying program functionality and analysing collected data.

activities.title: Data Integrity and Sensor Error Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach core data integrity concepts using professional QCAA terminology. activities.questioning:
Why might a micro:bit accelerometer record an unexpected 3G spike when placed gently on a desk? Expected: Environmental vibration or handling noise interfering with baseline calibration.
What is the difference between sensor drift and sampling error? Expected: Drift is a gradual calibration offset over time, while sampling error occurs when data points are collected too infrequently to capture rapid changes.
activities.scaffolding:
Full definitions for reference:
1. Data Integrity: The accuracy, consistency, and reliability of stored data throughout its lifecycle.
2. Signal: Meaningful physiological or kinetic movement data captured during a trial.
3. Noise: Irrelevant or random electrical/environmental disturbance corrupting a dataset.
4. Sensor Drift: Gradual deviation of sensor output from the true calibrated value over time.

workbookSpec.title: Data Cleaning Audit and Reflection
workbookSpec.prompt: Reflect on your data cleaning process. Document the key metrics of your dataset before and after cleaning, quantify the outliers identified, and justify the actions taken to ensure data integrity for subsequent analysis.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer:
Dataset Metrics Summary:
The raw dataset for my field trial contained 1200 rows of acceleration data. After applying filters to remove pre-trial setup and post-trial cool-down periods, the cleaned dataset now consists of 850 rows, directly representing the athlete's performance phase.

Outlier Identification and Treatment:
Using the logical query IF(OR(Acceleration_m/s2>2.5, Acceleration_m/s2<-0.5)), 7 data points were identified as outliers. 5 of these were removed as they represented sensor spikes inconsistent with human movement. The remaining 2 were retained as they were high-peak values consistent with maximum effort during a sprint and within physically plausible, albeit extreme, limits.

Justification of Data Cleaning Workflow:
My data cleaning workflow prioritised three critical steps to ensure data integrity and readiness for analysis. Firstly, unit conversion from milli-g to m/s² was performed to standardise measurements. Secondly, 'dead time' before and after the actual trial was systematically removed to isolate relevant performance data. Finally, logical queries were implemented to identify and manage outliers. These actions were essential to produce a dataset that accurately reflects athletic performance, free from noise and errors, enabling valid statistical analysis in subsequent stages. This process ensures the data aligns with the QCAA guidelines for data quality.

activities.title: Identifying Genuine Outliers vs. Hardware Glitches
activities.teacherDoes:
Model how to inspect a dataset visually to distinguish between an elite-level acceleration burst (genuine outlier) and a sensor disconnection spike (hardware glitch). Demonstrate how to apply conditional logic rules to flag values exceeding physiological thresholds.

Explicit Instruction: "When evaluating performance datasets in sports science, distinguishing real physiological extremes from measurement error is critical. Notice how an elite acceleration presents a smooth transition across adjacent timestamps, whereas a hardware glitch typically appears as an isolated, impossible vertical spike."

Worked Example: Display a scatter plot of GPS velocity data. "Observe point B4 at 18.2 m/s. We cross-reference the previous timestamp (8.1 m/s) and subsequent timestamp (8.3 m/s). Because humans cannot accelerate by 10 m/s instantaneously, we classify this as a sensor fault rather than an exceptional athletic effort."

First, open your 'Src' folder; verify the MakeCode .hex file version matches your latest build. Next, open your spreadsheet—toggle your slicers. If the charts do not update in real-time, your PivotTable data range is likely disconnected. Finally, ensure your raw .csv file is present; never overwrite raw data, as we require it for auditability. Check each box only when you have successfully interacted with the file.

orientate.smartStart: Students complete a pre-submission checklist in their workbook verifying all required digital artifacts are named correctly and stored in the submission directory.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can successfully package and submit my complete Sports Science Training project portfolio

activities.title: Final File Verification and Packaging
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the required folder structure and naming convention for the final project submission (e.g., Surname_Firstname_SportsScience_Portfolio). Model how to verify that all CSV files, Excel dashboards, and MakeCode hex files are intact. Emphasize that incomplete packaging directly impacts assessment verification under QCAA syllabus requirements.
activities.studentsDo: Organize your project files into the required folder structure and verify file integrity using the packaging checklist provided in your workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Check off each submission file requirement in your workbook checklist as you organize your local directory.
activities.questioning: What happens if an exported CSV file is modified in a text editor and saved with an incorrect delimiter before submission? Expected: Spreadsheet formulas and PivotTables will fail to parse columns correctly, corrupting data analysis and invalidating system verification.
activities.scaffolding: Required Submission Files: - MakeCode Hex file (.hex). - Raw field trial CSV dataset (.csv). - Cleaned analysis workbook (.xlsx). - Final critical evaluation and reflection report (.docx). Ensure all file extensions are visible and matching.
activities.eLearning: Laptops down for teacher file structure demonstration. Rear-of-room monitoring during individual file organization.
activities.transition: Transition from file organization to final submission portal upload in 3 minutes.

activities.workbookMaterials: Final Submission Packaging Checklist
activities.teacherAnswerKey: All five checklist items must be confirmed by the student prior to portal upload, ensuring absolute data integrity and adherence to QCAA assessment standards.

activities.title: Project Portfolio Submission
activities.teacherDoes:
Guide students through the final packaging and upload of their project portfolios to the school submission portal. Model how to verify file integrity and record the cryptographic submission receipt number. Address any network latency or archive compression errors proactively.

Example instruction: 'Ensure your root folder is compressed into a single ZIP file named using your Student ID and Surname. Once uploaded, copy the verification hash directly into your workbook.'
activities.studentsDo: Compress your completed project portfolio folder into a single ZIP archive, upload it to the designated portal, and record your verification details in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: Compress your portfolio into a ZIP file, upload it to the submission portal, and record your unique receipt code and unit reflection in your workbook.
activities.questioning: Why is recording a submission receipt number a vital digital citizenship practice in formal assessment contexts? Expected: It provides indisputable cryptographic proof of timely submission in the event of network routing errors or server timeouts.
activities.scaffolding:
Submission Protocol:
1. Verify all files (code, dashboard data, evaluation report) are present in the directory.
2. Right-click the folder and select 'Compress to ZIP file'.
3. Navigate to the portal submission link and attach the archive.
4. Click 'Confirm Submission' and immediately copy your transaction receipt code.
activities.eLearning: Monitor local network bandwidth and assist students encountering upload latency or compression anomalies.
activities.transition: Transition from submission upload to unit self-reflection in 2 minutes.

workbookSpec.title: Submission Record and Unit Reflection
workbookSpec.prompt: Record your official submission confirmation details and complete the structured reflection on your technical development throughout the unit.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Student records a valid transaction timestamp and confirmation hash. The technical challenge reflects a genuine debugging scenario (e.g., resolving asynchronous data logging intervals on the Micro:bit). The future improvement outlines a scalable engineering enhancement, such as implementing wireless telemetry via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE).

activities.title: Unit Debrief and Closure
activities.teacherDoes: Facilitate a brief whole-class debrief celebrating the completion of the sports science digital technologies unit. Model a reflective justification by stating: 'My rating is 5 because I successfully integrated hardware data capture with automated spreadsheet dashboards.' Direct students to complete the continuum scale and written justification in their workbook.
activities.studentsDo: Rate your confidence in applying digital technologies to solve real-world sports problems on the continuum scale in your workbook, providing a brief written justification for your rating.
activities.visibleInstructions: Rate your confidence in designing, programming, and analyzing data from a Micro:bit sports science system on the continuum scale in your workbook, then provide a written justification.
activities.questioning:
q: How has your understanding of data integrity changed from Week 1 to Week 10?
Expected: Moved from trusting raw sensor output blindly to implementing rigorous cleaning, logical validation, and anomaly flagging.
q: What core technical skill from this unit do you anticipate applying in future engineering or digital solutions?
Expected: Algorithm design for threshold detection and automated CSV data logging for performance metrics.
activities.scaffolding: Continuum Scale: 1 (Novice — require significant guidance) to 5 (Expert — confident in independent system design and data analysis). Justification sentence starter: 'I rated my confidence as [X] because I successfully demonstrated...'
activities.eLearning: Ensure all browsers are closed and devices are packed away securely.
activities.transition: Transition to lesson wrap-up and dismissal.

weeks.title: Hardware Setup and Data Acquisition
bullets: Explore Micro:bit V2 sensors for sports science applications.
Set up hardware to measure real-time movement data.
Analyse the data acquisition cycle: sensing, processing, outputting. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Problem Decomposition and User Stories
bullets: Conduct stakeholder interviews to identify performance requirements.
Decompose athletic metrics into specific technical specifications.
Draft user stories and establish functional design criteria. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Algorithmic Logic and Flowchart Design
bullets: Apply logical operators to define sensor threshold rules.
Design movement tracking algorithms using structured flowcharts.
Convert flowcharts into pseudocode and conduct peer reviews. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Micro:bit Programming and Real-Time Data
bullets: Translate algorithmic designs into functional MakeCode programs.
Implement object-oriented concepts for tracking physical movement.

weeks.title: Data Logging and Advanced Conditionals

Implement Micro:bit data logging for untethered field trials.

weeks.title: Field Testing and Data Collection
bullets: Conduct field trials to capture physical performance metrics.
Ensure data integrity across multiple physical activity trials.
Export logged movement datasets to raw CSV files. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Data Cleaning and Validation in Excel
bullets: Import raw CSV sports data into Microsoft Excel.
Apply logical queries to filter noise and flag outliers.
Convert raw sensor metrics into standardised measurement units. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Interactive Data Visualisation and Dashboards
bullets: Build interactive Excel dashboards using slicers and PivotCharts.
Visualise performance trends and identify athletic fatigue patterns.
Annotate charts to highlight key movement event thresholds. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: System Evaluation and Ethical Considerations
bullets: Evaluate digital solutions against initial user requirements.
Critique wearable tech ethics and athlete privacy concerns.
Document system reflections and propose future design enhancements. (Content available on Teams)

bullets: Finalise and submit the complete sports science portfolio.
Present interactive data dashboards in a class showcase.
Peer-review digital solution designs and data models. (Content available on Teams)
